name: Castor oil

lead: Castor oil is a thick, pale oil pressed from castor beans. In looksmaxxing circles people rub it on the scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes hoping for thicker, fuller-looking growth, and it also coats hair like a conditioner.

Proponents say it moisturises and thickens strands; its main component, ricinoleic acid, makes it very viscous. Its established medical use is as an oral stimulant laxative, and no clinical trial of castor oil for hair growth was found. Users report mixed results.

paras: People apply a small amount with fingertips or a clean spoolie to brows and lashes, or massage it into the scalp, often overnight, then wash out hair in the morning. It is used as a regular routine and often combined with other oils. Users who report changes describe waiting weeks to months.

Taken orally it commonly causes nausea, vomiting, cramping and diarrhoea, and labels advise against use with abdominal pain or in pre-term pregnancy. Oil near the eyes can irritate. Ricin from the raw bean is not present in the processed oil.

chain: Thick oil on hair, brows, lashes
angle.text: People rub castor oil on scalp, brows and lashes for thicker, fuller-looking growth, and the thick oil also coats hair like a conditioner. It is established as a laxative; no clinical trial has tested it for hair growth.

lead: Castor oil is a thick, pale vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of the castor plant, Ricinus communis, and about 90 percent of its fatty acids are ricinoleate [1]. It has been used for more than three millennia as a laxative and today is also an industrial raw material, a cosmetic emollient and a carrier in medicines [1][2].

In looksmaxxing and hair-care communities it is used as a topical oil on the scalp, beard, eyebrows and eyelashes. Proponents apply it nightly with a brush or fingertips, hoping for fuller-looking brows and lashes, thicker-looking hair and a conditioned shine; its viscosity also makes it a styling and sealing oil for some users [3][4][5]. Some combine it with rosemary oil, minoxidil or derma stamping, and some pair it with a prescription lash product [6][7][3].

A 2022 systematic review of coconut, castor and argan oils for hair in skin-of-colour patients covered 22 articles; it reported weaker evidence for castor oil improving hair luster and no strong evidence for growth, and noted that dermatologists often let patients continue hair oils because side effects are unlikely [8]. No clinical trial of castor oil for eyebrow, eyelash or scalp hair growth has been published [1][8].
Its established medical use is oral, as a stimulant laxative; the US label for an over-the-counter product lists temporary relief of occasional constipation [9].

paras: Castor oil is colourless to pale yellow with a distinct taste and odour, and it is unusually viscous for a vegetable oil [1]. Its triglycerides are dominated by ricinoleic acid, a hydroxylated fatty acid, with oleic and linoleic acids as the other notable components [1][2]. The hydroxyl group is what gives the oil its thickness, its stickiness on skin and its usefulness as a chemical feedstock [6][2].

Retail products come in several forms: plain pressed oil, solvent-free cold-pressed oil, and oil from roasted beans, often sold as Jamaican or 'black' castor oil. Hydrogenated castor oil appears as a thickener in personal-care products [1].

Castor oil is recorded as a laxative in the Ebers Papyrus, dated about 1550 BC, and was likely used earlier [1]. Its laxative action is attributed to ricinoleic acid released during digestion [1]. Nineteenth-century midwifery manuals recommended it for 'false pains', and it is still used for labour induction where modern drugs are unavailable [1].

Industrially it is a bio-based polyol for polyurethanes, coatings and foams, a precursor for chemicals such as sebacic acid and nylon-11 monomer, a low-temperature lubricant, a biodiesel feedstock and, historically, the main lubricant of First World War rotary aircraft engines [1][2]. The Turkey red oil derived from it was the first synthetic detergent after soap [1]. Food-grade forms serve as additives and in chocolate manufacture [1]. It is also a vehicle for some injected medicines [1].

A randomized trial examined topical periocular castor oil treatment for blepharitis, an eyelid condition [10]. Registered trials for castor oil concern labour induction and dental pulp response [11][12].

Cosmetically it acts as an emollient and carrier in lipsticks, hair conditioners and creams [1][6]. Wikipedia's overview of hair conditioners notes that natural oils have conditioned hair for centuries, and that modern products have largely replaced simple oils with silicones, fatty alcohols and polymers [13].

Hair oiling is a long-standing practice in Indian and African-heritage communities, and castor, coconut and argan oils are the commercially popular choices [8]. The 2022 review describes these oils as culturally rooted, and notes that dermatologists frequently advise continued use because adverse effects are rarely foreseen [8].

In looksmaxxing forums the oil is applied to eyebrows and eyelashes with a clean spoolie or mascara wand, to the beard and scalp as a massage oil, and sometimes to hair ends for gloss. Users often describe the routine as a low-cost companion to other hair or brow measures [3][7][14][15].

Proponents offer several explanations: that the oil moisturises and seals the shaft so hair breaks less, that massage improves scalp circulation, that ricinoleic acid has anti-inflammatory action and that the thick coating makes strands read as darker and denser. A looksmax.org thread title goes further and calls castor oil a 'legit collagen booster' [16]. These are users' proposals; the 2022 dermatology review found no strong evidence of growth effects [8].
For labour induction, a 2024 review said the mechanism is poorly understood and that a prostaglandin pathway has been suggested but not confirmed [1][17].

Taken by mouth, castor oil commonly causes nausea, vomiting, cramping and diarrhoea, and medical guidance discourages its use for simple constipation [1]. The US label advises against use when abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting are present unless directed by a doctor [9]. A pregnancy drug reference advises against oral or topical use in women who are pre-term pregnant [1].

Castor beans contain ricin, a toxic lectin, but heating during extraction deactivates it and it is not present in the finished oil [1][6]. A toxicology review describes ricin as dangerous mainly by inhalation or injection, with poor oral absorption and absorption through intact skin considered very unlikely [14]. The bean also contains an allergen, CB1A, that is neutralised during processing and is not in the oil [1].

Topical hair-use safety has not been the subject of dedicated trials; the review of hair oils states that side effects are not foreseen for these oils [8]. The American Cancer Society says evidence does not support claims that topical castor oil cures cancer or other diseases [1].

Seeds contain roughly 30 to 60 percent oil depending on source, and the oil is obtained by pressing or solvent extraction [1][6]. India is the largest producer [6]. A 1995 PNAS paper identified the oleate 12-hydroxylase enzyme in castor endosperm that creates ricinoleic acid, and a 2010 Nature Biotechnology paper published the plant's draft genome [15][18].

On looksmax.org, castor oil is most often discussed for eyebrows and eyelashes, sometimes combined with rosemary oil, minoxidil or derma stamping. Reports are mixed: one user described a month of nightly use followed by visibly longer lashes and a friend noticing thicker brows [4], while others report barely noticeable changes after a year [3]. A third thread acknowledges no strong evidence while suggesting it may at least coat brows like mascara [7]. Users also describe its thickness as awkward to apply [4].

Thread titles over several years show that the topic recurs: castor oil for eyelashes, castor oil with minoxidil, castor oil and derma stamping, castor oil for styling, and a post arguing it is 'the most misunderstood looksmax' that disparages minoxidil [19][20][21][22][23]. Both 'castor oil is legit' and 'castor oil is cope' positions are posted as thread titles [24][4][7].

No studies found on castor oil for hair, eyebrow or eyelash growth. A 2022 systematic review of 22 articles on coconut, castor and argan hair oils reported weaker evidence for castor oil improving hair luster, no strong evidence for hair growth, and no strong evidence for treating infestation; for coconut oil it found clinical evidence for brittle hair and infestation [8].

Registered clinical trials listed for castor oil concern labour induction in post-date pregnancy, including after previous caesarean, and dental pulp response [11][12]. A systematic review of three trials in 233 women reported insufficient evidence on labour induction, with all women taking it orally feeling nauseous [1]. A 2024 review of induction methods lists castor oil among complementary approaches [17]. A randomized trial studied it topically on the eyelid margins for blepharitis [10].
